props.title: Black Christmas

sections.content: The 2006 remake of Black Christmas (2006) represents a stark departure from Bob Clark's influential proto-slasher. While the original helped establish slasher conventions with its "calls are coming from inside the house" premise, the 2006 version directed by Glen Morgan opts for an excessive backstory involving Billy's yellow skin condition, cannibalistic tendencies, and family trauma. This shift exemplifies mid-2000s horror's obsession with explaining villain origins, similar to Rob Zombie's Halloween (2007) and The Texas Chainsaw Massacre: The Beginning (2006).

sections.content: The 2006 remake's excessive gore and elaborate death scenes reflect the torture porn era dominated by Saw (2004) and Hostel (2005). The film's attempts to modernize the material with more graphic violence and dark humor fall flat compared to other successful horror remakes of the period like The Hills Have Eyes (2006) and Dawn of the Dead (2004). The decision to expand Billy's backstory with incest and murder dilutes the original's effective minimalism. SUBHEAD: Holiday Horror Evolution

Black Christmas sits within a broader trend of holiday-themed horror films that peaked in the mid-2000s. While earlier entries like Gremlins (1984) and Christmas Evil (1980) balanced horror with dark comedy, the 2006 remake embraces pure shock value. This approach contrasts sharply with later Christmas horror films like Krampus (2015) and Better Watch Out (2016) that returned to a more balanced mix of scares and seasonal atmosphere.
